record.ear: Fair and cold. High 30. Low 17. Six inches at Whitestone; the Bowery Bay field cuts in two shifts.

lead.headline: Examiner finds the 10:31 Riverhead entry in a hand not Mr. Pruitt's
lead.deck: Mr. Carl Brandt: second entry matches none of the eight clerks' specimens; telephone company to name its lineman Monday
lead.body: Mr. Carl Brandt, the handwriting examiner, delivered his report on the counting-room ledger to Justice Rourke at 3:20 p.m. yesterday. He finds the Riverhead entry of 9:48 p.m. on the 6th to be in Mr. Walter Pruitt's hand, and the entry of 10:31 to be 'in a hand that matches none of the eight specimens supplied.' No specimen was supplied for the lineman. The New York Telephone Company is to give his name on Monday, when the Justice sits at 10.

columns.headline: Week's count: 2,410 tons of Sound ice cut at Whitestone
columns.body: The Bowery Bay Ice Company cut 2,410 tons on its Whitestone field in the six days to last night, working two shifts of 140 men from Wednesday. The ice measured six inches at dawn. The company's houses at College Point are one-third full.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships to sail from Dunedin tomorrow; City of New York to go under tow
columns.body: Commander Byrd's message, heard by the Navy at Bay Shore at 3:40 a.m., states that both ships sail for the ice tomorrow, Dunedin time, the Eleanor Bolling towing the City of New York to spare her coal. The dogs are aboard.

columns.headline: Arcade lights its Christmas windows at 5 tonight; shops open until 8
columns.body: The eleven shops of the Vantry Arcade will light their Christmas windows together at 5 p.m. today and remain open until 8 each evening until the 24th. The hardware counter has laid in 400 sleeves of valves and 60 crystal sets for the trade.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The elevated stops at Queensboro Plaza from 6 a.m. tomorrow. The Phonautograph Society begins recording on waking.

speaker.ear: Cold and getting colder. High 30. The ice is six inches and the ice men are smiling, which is unnatural.

lead.headline: Handwriting man reads the ledger and finds a hand nobody can hold
lead.deck: Pruitt wrote Riverhead at 9:48; somebody else wrote it at 10:31; the eight clerks are cleared of penmanship and the lineman has till Monday
lead.body: Mr. Brandt has looked at the ledger with a glass for a week and says this: Mr. Pruitt wrote Riverhead at 9:48, in his own round hand, and at 10:31 somebody wrote it again in a hand that belongs to none of the eight clerks. That leaves a lineman nobody wrote down, who came to fix an instrument and may have fixed rather more. We say nothing. The telephone company says his name on Monday. The Board says nothing at any hour.

columns.headline: Ice men cut 2,410 tons in a week and want the cold to stay on the line
columns.body: Two shifts on the Sound since Wednesday, six inches of ice, and the College Point houses a third full. The Bowery Bay company would like the weather to hold for another month. Everyone else in Queens would like a word with the Bowery Bay company.

columns.headline: Arcade switches on its Christmas windows; your wallet switches off
columns.body: Five o'clock tonight the eleven shops light up together and stay open till eight every night to Christmas Eve. The hardware counter has four hundred sleeves of valves and sixty crystal sets, which in this borough is how Santa Claus gets down the chimney.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will Byrd ring before he reaches the ice?'
columns.body: Madam, the Commander rings Bay Shore most mornings at about a quarter to four, and talks about coal. He sails tomorrow towed by his own second ship, to save coal. Expect a short call about coal. We will print it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The elevated stops at the Plaza tomorrow. The Society records everything tomorrow. Say nothing you want kept from 1978.

record.ear: Fair and colder. High 28. Low 15 expected tonight. Skating permitted on the Flushing ponds.

lead.headline: Byrd's ships sail from Dunedin for the ice; City of New York in tow
lead.deck: Expedition leaves at 9:15 a.m. New Zealand time after eight days ashore; Commander Byrd's farewell message played in the Record's window at 11:50 last night
lead.body: The City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling sailed from Port Chalmers, Dunedin, at 9:15 this morning, New Zealand time, for the Ross Sea, the Eleanor Bolling towing the larger ship to spare her coal. The 95 dogs are aboard in deck kennels. Commander Byrd's message, received by the Navy at Bay Shore and played in the Record's window at 11:50 last night to about 60 persons, ran three minutes. It thanked the people of Dunedin and gave the ships' coal.

columns.headline: Elevated's first Sunday stop at Queensboro Plaza today from 6 a.m.
columns.body: The Interborough will stop every Astoria and Corona train at Queensboro Plaza this morning from 6 until 1 p.m., the first regular Sunday service at the station. Guards will call the stop. The Transit Commission will station an observer on the platform.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society members begin recording 'one ordinary Sunday' today
columns.body: One hundred and eighty members of the Phonautograph Society of Queens record this Sunday in full, from waking to sleep, for sealing at Borough Hall to be played in 1978. The secretary, Mr. Cyril Abbot, reminds members that the day must be ordinary.

columns.headline: Flushing ponds opened to skaters; Parks Department posts the ice at five inches
columns.body: The Parks Department opened Kissena Lake and the Flushing ponds to skating at noon yesterday, the ice measuring five inches. Some 1,400 skated by dark. A boy who went through at the outlet was brought out by a chain of skaters in four minutes.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The New York Telephone Company has delivered a sealed letter to Justice Rourke's clerk. It is to be opened at 10 tomorrow.

speaker.ear: Cold and quiet. High 28. Mind what you say today; a hundred and eighty people are writing it down for 1978.

lead.headline: Byrd reverses the charges: his second ship tows him to the ice
lead.deck: The expedition leaves Dunedin on a rope to spare the coal; the farewell message runs three minutes, and two of them are thank-yous
lead.body: Commander Byrd has left New Zealand on the end of a rope. The Eleanor Bolling is towing the City of New York south so the big ship can keep her coal for the ice, which is the sort of economy we practise with the radiator. Sixty people heard the farewell in the Record's window at ten to midnight. He thanked Dunedin for a full two minutes, then gave the coal. Ninety-five dogs went aboard. Not one has written to thank Dunedin. Dogs know better.

columns.headline: Elevated stops at the Plaza today, and guards are told to call it out
columns.body: From six this morning until one, every Astoria and Corona train stops at Queensboro Plaza, as promised since September. The guards will call the stop. They have been practising on each other all week. The commission's man will stand on the platform with a pencil.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: an ordinary Sunday, and everyone on their best behaviour
columns.body: The Society records its whole Sunday today for 1978, and the Lady can report that forty members have bought new slippers, eleven have tuned the piano, and the secretary has asked his wife not to mention the brother-in-law. Nineteen seventy-eight will think Queens was tidy.

columns.headline: Boy goes through the ice at Flushing; fourteen skaters make a human cable
columns.body: The ponds opened at noon and by half past two a boy had found the thin bit at the outlet. Fourteen skaters lay down hand to ankle and had him out in four minutes, wet, blue and furious. Five inches is the posted figure. Skate in the middle.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The telephone company has sent the judge a sealed letter. Opens at ten Monday. The lineman's name is in an envelope, which is more than it was in the ledger.

record.ear: Clear and cold. High 27. Low 14 at 6 a.m., the coldest morning of the season.

lead.headline: Elevated stops at Queensboro Plaza 61 times on its first Sunday; 2,940 alight
lead.deck: Interborough reports no delay to through traffic; Transit Commission's observer enters the platform as 'crowded at 10, empty at 12'
lead.body: The Interborough stopped 61 Astoria and Corona trains at Queensboro Plaza between 6 a.m. and 1 p.m. yesterday, the first regular Sunday service at the station. The company counts 2,940 passengers alighting and 2,215 boarding. Through trains lost an average of 50 seconds. The Transit Commission's observer, Mr. Lyle Benning, entered the platform as 'crowded at 10, empty at 12' and recorded one complaint, from a Corona passenger who had not wished to stop. The service continues every Sunday.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society: 176 of 180 complete the ordinary Sunday; four sang
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society reports that 176 members recorded Sunday in full and four were withdrawn by the secretary for singing, three of them hymns. The records are to be delivered to Borough Hall on Thursday in a single copper case.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five beat the Paterson Crescents 31 to 24 at the armory
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club opened its basketball season at the Jackson Avenue armory on Saturday night with a victory of 31 to 24 over the Paterson Crescents before 1,300. The armory's record was kept. The club plays Bayonne on Saturday.

columns.headline: Telephone company's letter to be opened in chambers at 10 today
columns.body: Justice Rourke will open the New York Telephone Company's sealed letter, which names its lineman present in the Jamaica counting room at 10:31 on November 6, at the opening of this morning's hearing on Mr. Pruitt's petition. Mr. Brandt will be heard.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Fourteen degrees at 6 a.m. Coal yards report 900 orders before 8.

speaker.ear: Fourteen degrees. High 27. The coal man is the most popular person in Queens and knows it.

lead.headline: The Plaza finally makes the connection, sixty-one times in one morning
lead.deck: The elevated stops on a Sunday and the earth goes on turning; one man from Corona did not want to get off and was not made to
lead.body: Eleven years of asking, a mayor's circular and a forty-second trial, and yesterday the Astoria train stopped at Queensboro Plaza sixty-one times between six and one as if it had always meant to. Two thousand nine hundred and forty got off. The through passengers lost fifty seconds and complained for most of them. The commission's man wrote 'crowded at ten, empty at twelve,' which is also the Speaker's office on a Sunday. One gentleman from Corona objected to being stopped at all. We admire his consistency.

columns.headline: Four Society members cut off for singing on the ordinary Sunday
columns.body: A hundred and seventy-six recorded a whole day without incident. Four sang, three of them hymns and one of them in the bath, and the secretary has struck them off the record for 1978. We call that censorship. The future would have liked a hymn.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five shoots down Paterson, and the armory takes it down
columns.body: Thirty-one to twenty-four at the Jackson Avenue armory on Saturday, thirteen hundred in the gallery and every one of them on the armory's record shouting at the referee. Bayonne next Saturday. Bring a coat; the armory heats nothing but the argument.

columns.headline: Lineman's name in an envelope; the judge opens it at ten
columns.body: The telephone company has put its man's name in a sealed letter, as though he were a ballot. Justice Rourke opens it at ten this morning in front of everybody. We have a man in the corridor and another on the stairs, in case he runs.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Nine hundred coal orders before eight. The coal man has stopped taking calls and started taking bids.

record.ear: Fair and very cold. High 25. Low 12. The Sound is set from Whitestone to Throgs Neck.

lead.headline: Lineman named as Mr. Joseph Marchetti of Corona; resigned November 10
lead.deck: Justice Rourke issues a subpoena returnable December 17; Corona landlady tells process server he left 'with a valise and a receiving set'
lead.body: The New York Telephone Company's letter, opened by Justice Rourke at 10:04 yesterday, names its lineman present in the Jamaica counting room at 10:31 on November 6 as Mr. Joseph Marchetti, 34, of 41st Avenue, Corona. It states that he resigned on November 10. The Justice issued a subpoena returnable on December 17. The process server reported at 4 p.m. that Mr. Marchetti's landlady, Mrs. Rosa Bianchi, said he left on the 10th 'with a valise and a receiving set.' Mr. Brandt's report was entered.

columns.headline: Queens Light & Power declines Alderman Feeney's feeder test in writing
columns.body: The utility's chief engineer, Mr. Gustav Ober, wrote to Alderman Feeney yesterday that the company 'cannot interrupt supply to 31,000 consumers in December to measure a tone it does not produce.' The letter will be read at the committee's hearing on the 11th.

columns.headline: Radio Division returns the Astoria boy's crystal set; 'nothing received'
columns.body: The Federal Radio Division's inspector, Mr. Harold Pike, returned the crystal set of the eleven-year-old boy of 31st Street yesterday with a note that it had been listened to nightly for fourteen days 'and nothing received.' The boy says it worked for him.

columns.headline: Sound frozen across from Whitestone to Throgs Neck; ice seven inches
columns.body: The Sound was frozen from shore to shore between Whitestone and the Throgs Neck light at 7 a.m. yesterday, for the first time since 1920. The ice measured seven inches on the Bowery Bay field. The ferry to Clason Point has been suspended.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships 210 miles south of Dunedin at 3:20 a.m. Tow holding. Coal within estimate.

speaker.ear: Twelve degrees, and the Sound has frozen shut from shore to shore. High 25. So has the Board.

lead.headline: The lineman has a name, an address, and no forwarding number
lead.deck: Mr. Joseph Marchetti fixed the instrument at 10:31, quit four days later and walked out of Corona with a valise and a radio set
lead.body: The envelope opened at four minutes past ten and the lineman turned out to be Mr. Joseph Marchetti, thirty-four, of Corona, who resigned from the telephone company on November 10, four days after he was in the counting room with Riverhead coming in twice. The judge sent a man to Corona with a subpoena. The landlady says Mr. Marchetti left on the 10th with a valise and a receiving set, and paid up. Nobody in Queens pays up and leaves. It is the seventeenth now, or never.

columns.headline: Utility won't throw the switch on a tone it says it doesn't make
columns.body: Mr. Ober of Queens Light & Power has written to the Alderman that the company will not cut 31,000 homes in December to measure a hum it does not produce. That is the first time the company has used the word. It said 'tone.' We heard 'hum.'

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Not in the boy's crystal set, says the Division, which returns it
columns.body: Fourteen nights in a drawer at the Radio Division with a man listening, and the set received nothing. It went home to 31st Street yesterday. The boy plugged it in at supper and says he got the weather from Newark. He did not say he got WORS.

columns.headline: The Sound freezes solid and the Clason Point ferry is put on hold
columns.body: Shore to shore from Whitestone to the Throgs Neck light, the first time since 1920, and the ferry has been laid up. The ice is seven inches. A man from College Point walked to the Bronx at noon to prove it, and is there now.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd is 210 miles south, on a rope. The rope is holding. So is the coal.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 26. Ice eight inches on the Bowery Bay field. Wind north, light.

lead.headline: Sound ice harvest at full strength; 410 men on three fields
lead.deck: Bowery Bay, Knickerbocker and the College Point Ice Cooperative cut eight-inch ice; price to households held at 40 cents the hundredweight
lead.body: The ice harvest on the Sound reached full strength yesterday with 410 men and 22 horses working three fields between Whitestone and College Point. The Bowery Bay Ice Company, the Knickerbocker company and the College Point Ice Cooperative cut eight-inch ice from 7 a.m. and made the season's first household deliveries of Sound ice in Flushing by noon. The price to households is held at 40 cents the hundredweight. The Bowery Bay foreman, Mr. Owen Pratt, expects 'a full house by Christmas.'

columns.headline: Borough Hall writes a third time to Signal Ground Rents Inc.
columns.body: The Superintendent of Highways, Mr. Ludwig Haas, sent a third letter yesterday to Signal Ground Rents Inc., holders of the Vantry Arcade's ground rent, requiring the frozen downpipe on Jackson Avenue to be cleared by noon Thursday. Letters of November 14 and 26 were not answered.

columns.headline: Real estate owners retain Mr. Lucius Pell to oppose the Listening Act in Albany
columns.body: The Queens Real Estate Owners' Association has retained Mr. Lucius Pell of Jamaica to oppose Senator Harlan's Listening Act before the Judiciary Committee on January 9. Mr. Ambrose Tully said the association would send 'forty landlords and no walls.'

columns.headline: Byrd reports the first albatross; ships 480 miles out under tow
columns.body: The Navy's Bay Shore station heard the City of New York at 3:52 a.m., 480 miles south of Dunedin, still under tow. Commander Byrd reported a wandering albatross following the ships since Monday, a sea running moderate and the dogs well.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power to file a schedule with the Public Service Commission tomorrow. It declines to say what schedule.

speaker.ear: Cold and still. High 26. Eight inches of ice, and the ice men have stopped pretending to be sorry.

lead.headline: The ice men cut in on the Sound, and the line is eight inches thick
lead.deck: Four hundred and ten men, twenty-two horses and three companies saw the Sound into cubes; first delivery in Flushing by lunch
lead.body: Three ice companies went out on the Sound at seven yesterday with four hundred and ten men and twenty-two horses, none of them Dutchman, and by noon the first Sound ice of the year was sitting in a Flushing icebox, which is a short trip for a block of water. The price holds at forty cents the hundredweight, the companies say, out of the goodness of their hearts, which are also frozen. Mr. Pratt of Bowery Bay expects a full house by Christmas. So does the coal man.

columns.headline: Borough Hall rings the ground rent a third time; the ground lies low
columns.body: Signal Ground Rents Inc. has had two letters from Borough Hall about the Arcade's frozen downpipe and answered neither. Mr. Haas has sent a third, with a Thursday noon. The downpipe has made a skating rink on Jackson Avenue that the Parks Department did not authorise.

columns.headline: Landlords hire a lawyer for Albany: forty landlords, one Pell, no walls
columns.body: Mr. Tully's association has retained Mr. Lucius Pell of Jamaica to tell the Judiciary Committee on January 9 why walls should listen for free. Forty landlords are going. The walls are staying home, Mr. Tully says, which is the first time a landlord has left anything at home.

columns.headline: Byrd picks up an albatross; the dogs would like a word with it
columns.body: Four hundred and eighty miles south and still on the rope, and the Commander reports a wandering albatross following since Monday. Sailors say it is lucky. The dogs say it is lunch. The coal, for once, did not come up.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The utility files a 'schedule' tomorrow and will not say which. We have a guess, and it ends in cents.

record.ear: Cloudy, wind east. High 31. Light snow possible tonight.

lead.headline: Queens Light & Power files for a rate rise of half a cent
lead.deck: Schedule to the Public Service Commission would raise household rate to 7 1/2 cents from January 1; company cites 'cold-weather load'; Alderman Feeney asks for a hearing
lead.body: Queens Light & Power filed a new schedule with the Public Service Commission at 11:30 yesterday raising its household rate from 7 cents to 7 1/2 cents the kilowatt-hour from January 1. The company's filing cites 'the increase in cold-weather load across the borough.' Alderman Feeney, chairman of the committee hearing the Astoria petition, asked the Commission by telegram at 2:10 to hold a public hearing, observing that the company's load books 'have shown no change since September.'

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society opens its 1978 case to the borough: 'record something'
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society announced last night that its copper case at Borough Hall will receive records from any resident of Queens until March 1, on any subject under ten minutes. Mr. Cyril Abbot, secretary, asks the public to 'record something for 1978.' Records are taken at the Jamaica office.

columns.headline: Ordinary Sunday delivered to Borough Hall; 176 records in a copper case
columns.body: The Society's 176 records of Sunday last were carried into Borough Hall at 10 a.m. yesterday in a copper case of 140 pounds, borne by four members. The case was entered in the Borough's register and placed in the basement strong room, beside the tax rolls.

columns.headline: Arcade hardware counter sells 61 crystal sets in five days; valves 99 cents
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade's hardware counter reports 61 crystal sets sold since Saturday, one more than its stock, and has wired Newark for 100 more. The six-sleeve of receiving valves holds at 99 cents. Eggs are 64 cents at Dutch Kills market; coal 15 dollars.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships 690 miles south of Dunedin. Albatross still following. Dogs well.

speaker.ear: Grey, and snow maybe. High 31. The meter's running, and from January it runs faster.

lead.headline: Utility can't hear the hum but hears its own price loud and clear
lead.deck: Half a cent more the kilowatt-hour from New Year's Day, on account of a cold-weather load the company's own books say did not happen
lead.body: Fourteen volumes of no change since September, sworn to in Borough Hall, and yesterday Queens Light & Power filed for half a cent more the kilowatt-hour because of an increase in load. Alderman Feeney telegraphed the Public Service Commission at ten past two asking how a load can be unchanged on the 27th and increased on the 5th. The company says the cold. The books say nothing. The hum says 41 and asks for no rise at all, the only reasonable party in the matter.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society opens the line to 1978, ten minutes a call
columns.body: Any resident of Queens may now put ten minutes in the copper case at Borough Hall for 1978. Mr. Abbot asks the public to record something. The Society has never met the public. It will have a hundred thousand records about the landlord by Friday.

columns.headline: Ordinary Sundays go into the strong room beside the tax rolls
columns.body: Four members carried the case in, a hundred and forty pounds of copper and slippers and tidied pianos, and the Borough put it in the basement next to the tax rolls. Fifty years down there together. Only one of them will be any fun to open.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why is my crystal set sold out?'
columns.body: Sir, because the boy on 31st Street heard something on his and the whole of Astoria wants one. Sixty-one sold in five days, one more than in stock, which the counter cannot explain either. Newark is sending a hundred. Valves ninety-nine. A cent off a dollar.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's albatross is still following him. The utility's rate rise is following us. Only one of them is lucky.

record.ear: Snow ended, one inch. Clearing and colder. High 24. Low tonight 11.

lead.headline: Signal Ground Rents Inc. fails to answer Borough Hall a third time
lead.deck: Noon deadline passes in silence; the company's listed telephone rang 30 minutes without reply; highways men thaw the Arcade downpipe and bill the holders 14 dollars
lead.body: Signal Ground Rents Inc., holders of the Vantry Arcade's ground rent, made no answer by the Borough's deadline of noon yesterday to a third letter on the frozen downpipe at the Arcade's Jackson Avenue corner. The Queens exchange rang the company's listed number, at 120 Broadway, from 12:01 to 12:31 at Mr. Ludwig Haas's request without reply. At 1:15 a crew of the Highways Department thawed the pipe with braziers and sanded the pavement. A bill of 14 dollars was mailed at 4.

columns.headline: Mr. Marchetti's landlady heard; last rent paid to December 10
columns.body: Mr. Francis Gorman, for Mr. Pruitt, told the Record that Mrs. Rosa Bianchi of 41st Avenue, Corona, holds rent paid by Mr. Joseph Marchetti to December 10 and his room unentered. She says he 'was quiet and kept his set low.' The subpoena stands.

columns.headline: St. Rita's parish to record its Christmas pageant rehearsals for the children
columns.body: The pastor of St. Rita's, Long Island City, Father Ignatius Kerrigan, said yesterday that the parish system will record the children's Christmas pageant rehearsals each Thursday and play them back the same evening 'so that the shepherds may learn from the shepherds.' Sixty-two children take part.

columns.headline: Cold to settle through the week-end; Weather Bureau forecasts 9 degrees Sunday
columns.body: The Weather Bureau forecasts a low of 9 degrees on Sunday morning, which would be the coldest December reading in the borough since 1917. The Health Department asks householders to call on elderly neighbours and to keep the stove door shut at night.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The bill to Signal Ground Rents Inc. was posted at 4 p.m. at Long Island City. Postage 2 cents, charged to the Borough.

speaker.ear: An inch of snow and nine degrees coming Sunday. High 24. Put the cat in and the coal on.

lead.headline: Signal Ground Rents: all signal, no answer, third time running
lead.deck: Borough Hall writes three letters and rings for half an hour; the ground rent lets it ring, so the Borough brings its own braziers
lead.body: Three letters, two in November and one this week, and Signal Ground Rents Inc. has answered none of them, a perfect record. At one minute past noon the exchange rang the company's number at 120 Broadway and let it ring for thirty minutes, and nobody picked up, and nobody, the operator swears, was breathing on the other end either. So at a quarter past one the Highways men came with braziers and thawed the Arcade's downpipe themselves. The bill is fourteen dollars. Watch this space.

columns.headline: Marchetti paid his rent to the 10th and kept his set turned down low
columns.body: Mrs. Bianchi of Corona says her lineman lodger was quiet and kept his receiving set low, the two finest things a landlady can say of anyone. His rent runs to Monday. His room is untouched. If he wants it, he knows the number. He used to fix them.

columns.headline: St. Rita's will play the shepherds back to themselves every Thursday
columns.body: Father Kerrigan is to record the Christmas pageant rehearsals and play them to the children the same evening, so the shepherds may learn from the shepherds. Sixty-two children. We give the playback until the first giggle, and the giggle until the second shepherd.

columns.headline: Nine degrees on Sunday; the Bureau forecasts a cold snap and a loud one
columns.body: The Weather Bureau says nine on Sunday morning, the coldest December since 1917, and asks you to call on the old people next door. Call. Take coal. Keep the stove door shut at night. Pipes will be talking by Monday.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The bill went to Signal Ground Rents Inc. by the four o'clock post. The Borough paid the stamp. Of course it did.

record.ear: Clear and very cold. High 21. Low 10 at 7 a.m. Ice at Whitestone nine inches.

lead.headline: Ice cutter dies of blood poisoning; 410 men on the Sound stop work an hour
lead.deck: Mr. Michael Hanrahan, 31, of College Point, cut by a saw on the Bowery Bay field on the 1st; funeral Monday at St. Fidelis at 10
lead.body: Mr. Michael Hanrahan, 31, an ice cutter of the Bowery Bay Ice Company, died at Flushing Hospital at 4:40 a.m. yesterday of blood poisoning following a cut to the left hand by an ice saw on the 1st. Dr. Arthur Lowe said the infection 'was heard in the chest by Tuesday and could not be reached.' He leaves a wife and three children. The men on the three Sound fields stopped work from 11 to noon. The funeral is Monday at 10 at St. Fidelis, College Point.

columns.headline: Week's count: coal yards deliver 18,400 tons; price holds at 15 dollars
columns.body: The borough's coal dealers report 18,400 tons delivered in the week to last night, the most in any week since February 1926, with 71 horses and 40 motor trucks on the streets. The price holds at 15 dollars. The Vernon Avenue yard worked until 11 on Thursday.

columns.headline: Bowery Bay company opens a fund for the Hanrahan family; 212 dollars by evening
columns.body: The Bowery Bay Ice Company opened a fund for Mrs. Hanrahan and her children yesterday at its College Point office with 100 dollars of its own. The men on the three fields had added 112 dollars by 6 p.m. The Record will receive contributions at its Jackson Avenue counter.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships 900 miles south; the Eleanor Bolling to cast off tow at the pack
columns.body: Commander Byrd reports from 900 miles south of Dunedin that the City of New York will be cast off by the Eleanor Bolling at the edge of the pack ice and taken in by the whaler C. A. Larsen. The albatross left on Thursday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Ten degrees at 7 a.m. Nine expected tomorrow. The Health Department's telephone is open all night.

speaker.ear: Ten degrees at seven, and the milk is frozen on the step. High 21.

lead.headline: Cat takes over the Queens switchboard and puts the borough through by paw
lead.deck: A grey tabby moves onto the warm end of the board at the exchange; the operators route four positions around her and call her Party Line
lead.body: The warmest place in Queens this week is the end of the switchboard at the Queens exchange, where the valves run under the shelf, and a grey tabby from the alley has found it. She arrived on Monday, slept on position 40 until Wednesday, and is now on position 41, where the supervisor says the cords are 'warmer for some reason.' The operators route their calls around her. They call her Party Line. She has not put anybody through, but she has disconnected two.

columns.headline: The ice men lay down their saws for one of their own, and the line stands still
columns.body: Michael Hanrahan, thirty-one, of College Point, cut his hand on a saw on the 1st and died of it yesterday morning. Four hundred men stood still on the Sound for an hour. He leaves a wife and three children. We are taking money for them.

columns.headline: Eighteen thousand tons of coal in a week; the coal man finally hangs up his hat
columns.body: The yards delivered 18,400 tons this week, the most since 1926, and the price stayed at fifteen dollars, which the coal men think is a mistake. The Vernon Avenue yard worked until eleven on Thursday. Dutchman worked until ten and went home.

columns.headline: Byrd swaps tow lines for the pack; the albatross hangs up
columns.body: The Eleanor Bolling will let go at the pack ice and a Norwegian whaler will take the City of New York the rest of the way in, a long-distance connection with a change at the edge. The albatross left on Thursday. It had heard about the coal.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Nine degrees tomorrow. Bring the cat in. Bring the operator a cat.

record.ear: Clear and bitter. High 19. Low 8 at 6:30 a.m. Wind northwest, moderate.

lead.headline: Eight degrees at dawn, the coldest December morning in Queens since 1917
lead.deck: Exchange carries 312,000 calls by 9 a.m.; Health Department reports two deaths from exposure and 140 calls on frozen stoves; Sound ice ten inches
lead.body: The thermometer at the Long Island City courthouse read 8 degrees at 6:30 a.m. yesterday, the lowest December reading since 1917. The Queens exchange carried 312,000 calls by 9 a.m., most of them to coal yards, plumbers and the Health Department, which reports 140 calls on frozen stoves and two deaths from exposure, both of men without lodging, at the Hunters Point piers. The Sound ice measured ten inches at Whitestone. Some 3,000 skated on the Flushing ponds in the afternoon.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships sight the first icebergs at 59 south; dogs on deck to see them
columns.body: The Navy's Bay Shore station heard the City of New York at 3:14 a.m. reporting the first icebergs of the voyage, two tabular bergs at 59 degrees south, 'each larger than Queensboro Plaza.' The dogs were brought on deck to see them and barked for eleven minutes.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society receives 312 records for 1978 in three days
columns.body: The Society's Jamaica office received 312 records for the copper case between Thursday and last night. Mr. Abbot reports that 'about a third concern the weather, a third concern relations, and a third concern the Society.' The case will hold about 1,000.

columns.headline: Landlords' association to meet tomorrow night on the Albany delegation
columns.body: The Queens Real Estate Owners' Association meets tomorrow at 8 p.m. at the Elks' hall, Jamaica, to choose its forty delegates for the Listening Act hearing of January 9. Mr. Lucius Pell will speak. Members are asked to bring their system's installation papers, 'if they have any.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The St. Vincent de Paul Society opens the Vernon Boulevard hall to men without lodging from 8 tonight.

speaker.ear: Eight degrees, the coldest reception since 1917. High 19. Keep the stove door shut and your mouth too.

lead.headline: Eight degrees: Queens gets its coldest reception since the war
lead.deck: Three hundred thousand calls by nine o'clock and every one of them to a coal man, a plumber or a mother
lead.body: Eight degrees at half past six, and the exchange had three hundred and twelve thousand calls by nine, more than on election night, and nobody asked about Riverhead. They asked for coal, plumbers and the Health Department, which answered 140 frozen stoves. Two men with no roof died at the Hunters Point piers in the night, and we will say nothing clever about that. The St. Vincent de Paul hall opens at eight tonight. If you have a coat spare, it knows where to go.

columns.headline: Byrd's dogs meet their first iceberg and give it eleven minutes of static
columns.body: Two flat-topped bergs at fifty-nine south, each bigger than Queensboro Plaza, says the Commander, and the dogs were brought up to see them. They barked for eleven minutes. The bergs did not stop either. Byrd has seen the ice before the coal ran out. Progress.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: three hundred records for 1978, a third about the Society
columns.body: The Lady has the figures from Jamaica: a third of the records for the copper case are about the weather, a third about relations, and a third about the Phonautograph Society, mostly from members. Nineteen seventy-eight will know it was cold and that somebody's sister-in-law was impossible.

columns.headline: Landlords told to bring their papers; landlords hunt for their papers
columns.body: Mr. Tully's association meets tomorrow night in Jamaica and members are asked to bring their building system's installation papers, if they have any. Most systems in Queens went in before anybody wrote anything down. The papers will be brief. The meeting will not.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Party Line the exchange cat has moved to position 42. The supervisor says 41 'went cold.'

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 24. Low 12. Ice on the Sound eleven inches.

lead.headline: Ice field watchman reports WORS 1610 on shanty receiver at 3:12 a.m. Sunday
lead.deck: Mr. Daniel Rooney of the Bowery Bay company says the station was strongest at the middle of the field; Radio Division walks the ice with a loop at noon, hears nothing
lead.body: Mr. Daniel Rooney, night watchman on the Bowery Bay Ice Company's Whitestone field, reported at 3:20 a.m. yesterday that the field shanty's receiving set had carried a station announcing itself as WORS 1610 from 3:12 until 3:17. He says the signal grew louder as he carried the set toward the middle of the field. The Federal Radio Division's Mr. Harold Pike walked the field at noon with a loop receiver and heard nothing. Mr. Rooney has kept the set.

columns.headline: Athletic Club five lose to Bayonne 28 to 26; armory record played on a foul
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club lost to the Bayonne Pioneers 28 to 26 at the Jackson Avenue armory on Saturday before 1,600. A foul in the last minute was disputed, and the armory record was played at the scorer's table. The referee's call stood.

columns.headline: Valves reach six for a dollar at the Arcade counter; eggs 65, coal 15
columns.body: The Arcade hardware counter marked the six-sleeve of receiving valves at one dollar on Saturday morning, up a cent, the first dollar sleeve in Queens since 1926. Eggs are 65 cents the dozen at Dutch Kills market. Coal holds at 15 dollars the ton.

columns.headline: Hanrahan funeral at St. Fidelis at 10 today; ice fields closed till 1
columns.body: The funeral of Mr. Michael Hanrahan will be held at 10 a.m. today at St. Fidelis, College Point. The three ice companies close their Sound fields until 1 p.m. The family fund at the Record's counter and the company office stood at 641 dollars last night.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Hum committee sits tomorrow at 2 p.m. at Borough Hall. Thirty-nine speakers remain.

speaker.ear: Twelve degrees and an inch more ice. High 24. The valve is a dollar. We told you.

lead.headline: Where's WORS? On thin ice, says the Whitestone watchman
lead.deck: Five minutes at twelve past three on the shanty set, louder toward the middle of the Sound; the Division walks it with a loop and hears skates
lead.body: Dan Rooney sits up all night in a shanty on the ice with a stove, a lantern and a receiving set, and at twelve past three on Sunday the set said WORS 1610 and played something for five minutes. Dan carried it onto the field, and it got louder. He stopped at the middle, where the ice is eleven inches and the water is forty feet, and decided that was far enough. The Division's Mr. Pike walked the field at noon with a loop and heard skates.

columns.headline: Bayonne beats the Club by a basket, and the armory plays back the foul
columns.body: Twenty-eight to twenty-six, and in the last minute the Club's centre was called for a foul he swears he never made. The scorer played the armory record at the table. It contained sixteen hundred people swearing the same thing. The call stood.

columns.headline: The dollar sleeve arrives on schedule; the counterman takes a bow
columns.body: Six valves for a dollar on Saturday morning, as promised since Thanksgiving, and the counterman says he has never been happier to be right. Eggs sixty-five. Coal fifteen. The Speaker one cent, which is the only thing in Queens that has not moved since the war.

columns.headline: College Point buries an ice cutter today, and the Sound is quiet for him
columns.body: Michael Hanrahan's funeral is at ten at St. Fidelis. The three fields close until one, so there will be no saws on the Sound this morning. His family's fund stands at six hundred and forty-one dollars. Our counter is still open.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The hum gets its second hearing tomorrow at two. Thirty-nine speakers. The hum is not speaking.

record.ear: Cloudy and cold. High 27. Snow likely tomorrow afternoon.

lead.headline: Hum committee resumes at 2 today; utility's refusal of feeder test to be read
lead.deck: Thirty-nine speakers remain from November 27; Alderman Feeney to move that the Public Service Commission hear the Hum with the rate case
lead.body: The committee of Alderman Feeney, Dr. Ruth Albrecht and Mr. Oskar Lind resumes its hearing on the Astoria petition at 2 p.m. today in the Borough Hall chamber. The 39 speakers not reached on November 27 will be heard at five minutes each. Mr. Gustav Ober's letter declining a ten-minute cut of the Astoria feeder will be read first. Alderman Feeney said yesterday he will move that the Public Service Commission take up the Hum in its hearing on the company's rate schedule.

columns.headline: Postcard signed 'J. Marchetti' received by Justice Rourke's clerk
columns.body: A postcard signed 'J. Marchetti' and postmarked Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, December 8, reached Justice Rourke's clerk yesterday. It reads in full: 'I fixed the instrument and went home.' The card has been sent to Mr. Carl Brandt. The subpoena stands for the 17th.

columns.headline: Hanrahan funeral: 600 at St. Fidelis; ice cutters carry the coffin
columns.body: About 600 attended the funeral of Mr. Michael Hanrahan at St. Fidelis, College Point, at 10 yesterday. Six ice cutters of the Bowery Bay company carried the coffin. The Requiem was recorded by the parish at the family's request. The fund stands at 803 dollars.

columns.headline: Arcade shops to stay open until 9 from today; Saturday hours until 10
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade's eleven shops will remain open until 9 p.m. from today to the 24th, and until 10 on the two Saturdays, the Chamber of Commerce reports. The luncheonette will serve until the last shop closes. The hardware counter has no crystal sets until Thursday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships met the whaler C. A. Larsen at 3:30 a.m. at the pack edge. Tow transferred.

speaker.ear: Grey and cold. High 27. The hum's day in court resumes at two, and it still has no lawyer.

lead.headline: Hum hearing back on the line at two, and the utility's 'no' goes first
lead.deck: Thirty-nine Astorians still waiting to speak; the Alderman wants the hum tried alongside the rate rise, where the company cannot hang up on it
lead.body: The committee sits again at two with thirty-nine speakers left from the 27th, and the first thing read will be Mr. Ober's letter saying the company will not switch off Astoria for ten minutes to measure a tone it does not make. Then the Astorians. Then the Alderman, who wants the Public Service Commission to hear the hum in the same room as the half-cent rise, on the principle that a company asking for more money ought to be able to hear something.

columns.headline: The lineman drops a line: 'I fixed the instrument and went home'
columns.body: A postcard from Wilkes-Barre reached the judge's clerk yesterday, signed J. Marchetti, eight words long. He fixed the instrument and went home. Which instrument, which home, and why Riverhead rang twice, he does not say. The card has gone to the handwriting man.

columns.headline: Six ice men carry one of their own; College Point stands in the cold
columns.body: Six hundred at St. Fidelis yesterday for Michael Hanrahan, and his own crew carried him. The parish recorded the Mass for his children. The fund is past eight hundred dollars. Thank you, Queens. That is the whole of this column.

columns.headline: Arcade open till nine; your husband has no excuse till ten on Saturday
columns.body: The eleven shops stay open till nine every night to Christmas Eve and till ten on Saturdays, the luncheonette serving to the last. No crystal sets till Thursday. If he says he was at the Arcade buying you a crystal set, Madam, he was not.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd has changed tow at the pack edge, from his own ship to a whaler. A transfer, as the operator says.

record.ear: Cloudy, snow by afternoon, two to three inches. High 29.

lead.headline: Hum committee asks the Public Service Commission to order the feeder test
lead.deck: Thirty-nine speakers heard in 3 hours 20 minutes; a Ditmars Avenue baker plays a cellar record of 1913; resolution carried 3 to 0
lead.body: The committee on the Astoria petition heard its remaining 39 speakers in the Borough Hall chamber from 2:05 to 5:25 yesterday. Mr. Konrad Hesse, a baker of Ditmars Avenue, played a record of his cellar made in 1913, which the committee's meters read at 41 cycles. Queens Light & Power was not represented. At 5:40 the committee resolved, 3 to 0, to ask the Public Service Commission to order a ten-minute cut of the Astoria feeder and to hear the Hum with the rate schedule.

columns.headline: First Astoria train fitted with contact shoe heaters; tried on the Plaza curve
columns.body: The Interborough ran the first Astoria train fitted with electric heaters on its contact shoes over the Queensboro Plaza curve at 1 a.m. yesterday in 18 degrees. The shoes held the rail. The company says all Astoria and Corona trains will be fitted by December 31.

columns.headline: Postcard in Mr. Marchetti's hand, says Mr. Brandt; ledger entry 'not compared'
columns.body: Mr. Carl Brandt told Justice Rourke's clerk yesterday that the Wilkes-Barre postcard matches the specimen signature in Mr. Joseph Marchetti's telephone company file. He has not compared it with the ledger entry of 10:31 'and will not, without an order.' The Justice is asked for one.

columns.headline: St. Rita's shepherds rehearse Thursday; parish to play the record at 7
columns.body: St. Rita's parish, Long Island City, holds the first rehearsal of its Christmas pageant tomorrow at 4 p.m., with 62 children. Father Ignatius Kerrigan says the record will be played back to the children and their parents at 7 in the parish hall.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power says it 'was not invited to attend, having already written.'

speaker.ear: Snow this afternoon. High 29. The hum was played from 1913 last night, and it had not changed its tune.

lead.headline: Baker brings a cellar from 1913, and the hum is already on the record
lead.deck: Mr. Hesse of Ditmars Avenue plays a fifteen-year-old record and the meters say 41; the committee sends the switch to the Public Service Commission
lead.body: Thirty-nine speakers, and the one who mattered was a baker. Mr. Hesse of Ditmars Avenue put a record on the committee table that he made of his cellar in 1913, to settle a question of mice, and the two meters read it at 41 cycles. Nineteen thirteen. The utility said the hum started in September, or rather it said there was no hum, starting in September. The utility was not there. The committee voted three to nothing to ask the Commission to pull the switch.

columns.headline: The elevated warms its feet at last, and holds the curve at one in the morning
columns.body: The first train with heated contact shoes went round the Plaza curve at one yesterday morning in eighteen degrees and did not stop until it meant to. Every Astoria and Corona train will have warm shoes by New Year's Eve. The passengers' remain your affair.

columns.headline: Handwriting man says the postcard is Marchetti's but won't put it on the line
columns.body: Mr. Brandt says the card from Wilkes-Barre matches the lineman's signature on file. Asked whether it matches the 10:31 entry in the ledger, he says he has not compared them and will not without an order. A careful man. Mr. Gorman is asking the judge for an order.

columns.headline: St. Rita's shepherds go on the record Thursday; parents get the playback
columns.body: Sixty-two children rehearse the Christmas pageant at four tomorrow, and the parish will play it back to them and their parents at seven. Father Kerrigan believes the shepherds will learn from hearing themselves. Father Kerrigan has not heard sixty-two children before.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The utility was not at the hearing, 'having already written.' So, in 1913, had the baker.

record.ear: Snow ended, three inches. Fair and cold. High 26.

lead.headline: Arcade toy counter sells out of answering dolls; 140 orders taken for Newark
lead.deck: Doll with a six-word record at 3 dollars 50 'the season's article,' Chamber of Commerce reports; Arcade trade 31 per cent above the first fortnight of November
lead.body: The Vantry Arcade's toy and stationery shop sold its last answering doll at 6:40 last night, eleven days after the line was put in the window. The doll, at 3 dollars 50, carries a record of six words and plays them when its hand is pressed. The shop has taken 140 orders for delivery from Newark by the 22nd. The Chamber of Commerce reports Arcade trade 31 per cent above the first fortnight of November. The luncheonette reports the booth telephone in use 'continuously.'

columns.headline: Commission to hear rate schedule and the Hum together January 15
columns.body: The Public Service Commission announced at 3 p.m. yesterday that it will hear Queens Light & Power's rate schedule and the Astoria committee's request for a feeder test together on January 15 at its Manhattan offices. The proposed rate is suspended until then.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships in the pack ice at 64 south; Larsen breaks a lane
columns.body: Commander Byrd reports from 64 degrees south that the whaler C. A. Larsen is breaking a lane through loose pack for the City of New York, making four knots. The Eleanor Bolling has turned back to Dunedin for coal. The dogs are kept below in the ice.

columns.headline: Dutchman stops at eleven houses on his 1925 round; two customers moved
columns.body: The Percheron Dutchman, hauling coal from the Vernon Avenue yard since November 26, has stopped of his own accord at eleven houses on his round of 1925, the foreman Mr. Anton Keller reports. Nine still take coal from the yard. Two moved in 1926.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Justice Rourke has ordered Mr. Brandt to compare the postcard with the 10:31 entry. Report by the 17th.

speaker.ear: Three inches and quiet under it. High 26. Every child in Queens wants a doll that talks back, as if they lacked practice.

lead.headline: Answering doll sells out; the Arcade can't get Newark on the line fast enough
lead.deck: Three-fifty buys six words and a china face; a hundred and forty little girls are waiting and their mothers are on the luncheonette telephone
lead.body: It says six words when you squeeze its hand, and for three dollars and fifty cents Queens has decided that is a bargain, because the last answering doll went out of the Arcade at twenty to seven last night and the shop has a hundred and forty orders waiting on Newark. Trade is up thirty-one per cent. The luncheonette booth has not been empty since Saturday. We have heard the doll. The six words are 'Good night, I am listening, Mother.' We wish they had chosen five.

columns.headline: Commission puts the hum and the half-cent on the same line, January 15
columns.body: The Public Service Commission will hear the rate rise and the feeder test in one room in January and has suspended the rise until then. So the company can have its half-cent when it lets Astoria go dark for ten minutes. That is called a party line.

columns.headline: Byrd hits the pack and the whaler cuts a lane, four knots, no waiting
columns.body: Sixty-four south and the ice closes in, and the Norwegian whaler is breaking a road for the City of New York at four knots. The Eleanor Bolling has gone back for coal. Of course it has.

columns.headline: Dutchman keeps his old round, and two of his customers moved in 1926
columns.body: The horse stops at eleven houses he served in 1925 without being asked, and nine of them still want coal. At the other two he waits a minute and walks on. Mr. Keller says Dutchman never had a wrong number in his life, only a stale one.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The judge has ordered the handwriting man to compare the postcard with the 10:31 entry. Report by Monday. We are holding.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 25. Low 13. The Sound ice twelve inches at Whitestone.

lead.headline: St. Rita's children hear their pageant rehearsal played back
lead.deck: Sixty-two children and 90 parents in the parish hall at 7; second shepherd's lines 'much improved on hearing'; Sister Bernadette lays an extra amen to the organ
lead.body: St. Rita's parish, Long Island City, recorded its first Christmas pageant rehearsal from 4 to 5:10 p.m. yesterday and played it back to the 62 children and about 90 parents in the parish hall at 7. Father Ignatius Kerrigan said the second shepherd 'improved on hearing himself.' Sister Bernadette, who directs, said the record contains 'one more amen than there were children,' which she laid to the organ. The pageant will be performed on the 23rd at 4 and recorded for the parish.

columns.headline: Senator Harlan's revised Listening Act to the printer; fee set at 4 dollars
columns.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's office sent the revised Listening Act to the State printer at Albany yesterday with the licence fee set at 4 dollars a building. Mr. Ambrose Tully said the association's objection 'remains in principle and is now one dollar smaller.'

columns.headline: Byrd's ships cross the Antarctic Circle at 2:10 a.m. in the pack
columns.body: The Navy's Bay Shore station heard the City of New York report crossing the Antarctic Circle at 2:10 a.m. yesterday, Eastern time, under tow of the C. A. Larsen through heavy pack. Commander Byrd says the ships have daylight for 22 hours.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society's records for 1978 pass 800; second case ordered
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society reports 816 records received for its Borough Hall case since the 6th. Mr. Cyril Abbot says a second copper case has been ordered from a Long Island City coppersmith and that the Society 'did not anticipate the borough.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Brandt carried the Marchetti postcard and the ledger to chambers at 4 p.m. He will report Monday.

speaker.ear: Twelve inches of ice and a clear sky. High 25. Sixty-two shepherds heard themselves last night, and the angels want a better reception.

lead.headline: Pageant on playback: the shepherds hear themselves and ask for another take
lead.deck: St. Rita's plays the rehearsal back to sixty-two children; the second shepherd remembers his lines; Sister Bernadette counts the amens and gets one too many
lead.body: St. Rita's recorded its Christmas pageant rehearsal yesterday and played it back to the cast at seven, with ninety parents in the hall pretending not to be proud. The second shepherd, who forgot everything at four, heard himself forget it and by half past seven had it cold. The ox asked for his moo to be played twice. Sister Bernadette counted one more amen on the record than there were children, and laid it to the organ, as nuns have been doing since organs. The real thing is the 23rd.

columns.headline: Listening Act goes to the printer, and the walls drop to four dollars
columns.body: Senator Harlan has sent his bill to the printer at four dollars a building, so the walls have come down a dollar since November. Mr. Tully says his objection remains in principle and is now a dollar smaller. At this rate the walls will pay him by Easter.

columns.headline: Byrd crosses the Circle, and the sun stays on the line twenty-two hours
columns.body: The Antarctic Circle at ten past two, on the end of a whaler's rope, through heavy pack, with daylight for twenty-two hours. The Commander has more sun than he can use and less coal than he wants. Queens has the reverse.

columns.headline: Society gets 816 calls for 1978 and orders a second box; future overbooked
columns.body: The copper case is full and Mr. Abbot has ordered another one, saying the Society did not anticipate the borough. Nobody ever does. Eight hundred and sixteen records in eight days, and the Lady hears there are forty about the luncheonette's coffee.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The handwriting man has the postcard and the ledger side by side. Monday. Nobody breathe.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 28. Low 15. Twelve inches at Whitestone; the harvest continues.

lead.headline: Week's count: 9,640 tons of Sound ice housed; harvest the largest since 1920
lead.deck: Three companies report 21,400 tons since November 24; College Point houses full; Bowery Bay opens a second field off Willets Point
lead.body: The three ice companies on the Sound housed 9,640 tons in the week to last night and 21,400 tons since cutting began on November 24, the largest harvest at this date since 1920. The Bowery Bay Ice Company's College Point houses were filled on Thursday, and the company opened a second field of nine acres off Willets Point yesterday with 90 men. The ice measured twelve inches. Mr. Owen Pratt, foreman, said the men had worked 'with Mr. Hanrahan's saw hung in the shanty.'

columns.headline: Signal Ground Rents Inc. bill of 14 dollars neither paid nor returned
columns.body: The Borough's bill of 14 dollars to Signal Ground Rents Inc. for thawing the Arcade downpipe, posted on the 6th, has been neither paid nor returned by the Post Office, Mr. Ludwig Haas reports. The downpipe froze again on Thursday night and was thawed yesterday.

columns.headline: Arcade traffic counted: 41,200 persons in the week; the Saturday hours begin
columns.body: The Chamber of Commerce's count of persons entering the Vantry Arcade, taken from the Arcade's own system, was 41,200 for the week ending last night, against 17,900 in its first week. The shops open until 10 tonight. The answering dolls arrive on the 20th.

columns.headline: Party Line, the exchange cat, to be kept; supervisor's request granted
columns.body: The New York Telephone Company has granted the Queens exchange supervisor's request that the grey cat living at position 42 of the switchboard be kept 'for the control of mice,' and allowed a saucer. The operators report she has disconnected no call since Tuesday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships at 67 south, through the heaviest pack. Coal within estimate. Ross Sea expected before Christmas.

speaker.ear: Cold and clear. High 28. The Sound is a warehouse now, and the ice men are rich men in wet boots.

lead.headline: Ice men put 21,400 tons on hold and open a second line at Willets Point
lead.deck: Biggest harvest since 1920, College Point full to the rafters, and a dead man's saw hanging in the shanty where the crew can see it
lead.body: Twenty-one thousand four hundred tons of the Sound are now sitting in sawdust at College Point, the biggest harvest since 1920, and the houses are so full that Bowery Bay has opened a second field off Willets Point with ninety men. The ice is a foot thick. You could drive the elevated across it, and somebody will try. Mr. Pratt says the crews work with Michael Hanrahan's saw hung up in the shanty. Nobody uses it. Nobody has asked to.

columns.headline: The ground rent's bill comes back to nobody; the downpipe freezes again
columns.body: Fourteen dollars for thawing a downpipe, posted to Signal Ground Rents Inc. a week ago, neither paid nor sent back, which means somebody at 120 Broadway has it and is saying nothing. The pipe froze again on Thursday. The Borough thawed it again. That will be twenty-eight dollars.

columns.headline: Forty-one thousand through the Arcade, every one of them counted by ear
columns.body: The Arcade's own system counted 41,200 persons through the doors this week, against 17,900 in its first. The Chamber does not explain how a system counts people. It counts footsteps and divides by two. Open till ten tonight. Answering dolls on the 20th.

columns.headline: Party Line gets the job: the company hires the cat and gives her a saucer
columns.body: The telephone company has agreed that the grey cat on position 42 may stay, for the control of mice, with a saucer. She has disconnected nobody since Tuesday and caught one mouse, which she brought to the supervisor. Hold the line, Party. You're through.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd is at sixty-seven south, in the thickest pack yet. The Ross Sea by Christmas, he says. Santa is closer.
